rules.mechanism: Totally stop the sit-ups and crunches.
rules.note: Sit-up and crunch family load the disc in repeated loaded flexion, the exact motion flexion-intolerant herniation patients are told to stop. No pattern tag covers this family (Sit-Up, Crunch, Russian Twist, Barbell Good Morning and others carry patterns: null in the catalog), so name_regex was required. Sourced (loaded flexion mechanism), unreviewed.

rules.mechanism: Twisting while you lift can also make your back vulnerable. Rotation stresses the disc.
rules.note: Loaded and unloaded trunk rotation both stress an already herniated disc per AAOS and the flexion-intolerance literature. Russian Twist carries no pattern tag in the catalog (patterns: null), so name_regex covers it alongside the trunk-rotation pattern set. Sourced (rotation/twisting mechanism), unreviewed.

rules.mechanism: Make all your physical activity slow and controlled (steady), especially bending forward and lifting.
rules.note: Deadlift, good-morning, and rack-pull variants are, by definition, loaded forward bending under a lifted load, the mechanism AAOS names as aggravating. A blanket hip-hinge pattern rule would also sweep in low-flexion, low-risk hinge work (hip thrust, glute bridge) the mechanism does not name, so name_regex targets the loaded-forward-bend lift family specifically instead of the hip-hinge pattern. Sourced (loaded forward-bend lifting mechanism), unreviewed. The AAOS sentence asks for slow, controlled bending and lifting rather than forbidding it; this rule stands on the curated tier, which already contraindicates the conventional and Romanian deadlift, block pull, Zercher good morning and back squat for this injury, so the remaining deadlift, good morning and rack pull variants follow the movement class a human established. Sourced (mechanism), unreviewed.

Acute-phase guidance excludes contact sports outright and subacute guidance separately names football, rugby, and martial arts; the catalog's takedown-sprawl, striking, and rotational-strike patterns are the contact/combat-sport drills (Sambo takedowns, HEMA grapple entries, Krav Maga, Kendo, Karate). Whiplash's own mechanism is a forceful head snap, which contact and grappling entries directly risk reproducing. Sourced (contact/martial-arts avoidance), unreviewed. Source is a clinic page rather than a clinical reference; kept because avoiding contact and jarring impact in acute whiplash is standard first-line advice, and flagged for a reputable citation. Sourced (mechanism, weak source), unreviewed.

rules.mechanism: Avoid running, jumping, or jarring movements
rules.note: Jarring landings transmit an impact through the trunk into the neck, echoing the acceleration-deceleration mechanism of whiplash itself. Running alone (locomotion pattern) is not included since the source names it alongside jumping/jarring, not as a standalone restriction, and locomotion covers far more than running. Sourced (jarring-impact mechanism), unreviewed. Source is a clinic page rather than a clinical reference; kept because avoiding contact and jarring impact in acute whiplash is standard first-line advice, and flagged for a reputable citation. Sourced (mechanism, weak source), unreviewed.

rules.mechanism: This can occur in ipsilateral shoulder depression and neck deviation towards the contralateral side, often seen in tackling, which causes stretching of the brachial plexus on the ipsilateral side.
rules.note: The traction mechanism (shoulder driven down while the neck is forced the other way, seen in tackling/wrestling takedowns) is reproduced by the catalog's takedown-sprawl drills (Sambo takedown rehearsal and belt-grip entry, HEMA grapple-throw entry, roll and break-fall practice), all of which load the shoulder and neck together under a fall or grip contest. Sourced (traction/tackling mechanism), unreviewed.

rehab_early.note: AAOS: doctor or physical therapist may recommend a simple walking program while recovering. Plain Walking (not the loaded Rucking variant) matches this. Sourced (walking program), unreviewed.

McGill's side bridge/side plank is one of the Big Three, framed as building a pain-free foundation before more activity; Side Plank (anti-lateral-flexion) is the catalog match. Curl-up and bird dog are not in the 575-exercise catalog (bird dog is item 4's catalog gap), so only Side Plank is added here. Sourced (McGill Big Three, side bridge), unreviewed.

research:
Lumbar disc herniation (id 20). Primary source www.orthoinfo.org/en/diseases--conditions/herniated-disk-in-the-lower-back/ (AAOS OrthoInfo, redirected from orthoinfo.aaos.org): "Twisting while you lift can also make your back vulnerable.", "Using your back muscles instead of your legs to lift heavy objects can cause a herniated disk.", "Make all your physical activity slow and controlled (steady), especially bending forward and lifting.", "Your doctor or a physical therapist may recommend a simple walking program (such as 30 minutes each day)." NOT ON PAGE: no explicit exercise list. Second source dynamicchiropractic.com/article/56837-flexion-intolerant-lower-back-pain-part-1-diagnosis: "Totally stop the sit-ups and crunches.", "Rotation stresses the disc.", "Prolonged sitting creates migration of the disc material posteriorly, irritating the sensitive annulus.", "They cannot do yoga-style prolonged flexion.". Third source acefitness.org/resources/pros/expert-articles/7077 (McGill's Big Three): curl-up, side bridge, and bird dog descriptions quoted verbatim; "designed to build a pain-free foundation for more activity"; NOT ON PAGE for explicit "safe while symptomatic" language, inferred from framing plus McGill's broader flexion-intolerance protocol (corroborated by the dynamicchiropractic source, which is a McGill-derived clinical summary). physio-pedia.com/Lumbar_Disc_Herniation returned HTTP 403 (bot-blocked), so Physiopedia's own disc-herniation page could not be quoted; AAOS + the McGill-derived sources cover the same mechanism (loaded/repeated flexion and rotation) so the rules did not depend on it. Curl-up and bird dog are NOT in the 575-exercise catalog (bird dog is scoped to item 4, catalog gaps), so only Side Plank (132, matching McGill's side bridge) and Walking (1110, matching the AAOS walking-program line) were added to rehab_early.

Whiplash (id 60). physio-pedia.com/Whiplash_Associated_Disorders and mayoclinic.org both returned HTTP 403. my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/11982-whiplash gave the mechanism: "Whiplash happens when your head forcefully goes backward and then forward.", "That makes your neck compress or extend too quickly. It pushes the muscles, ligaments and bones of your spine beyond what they can handle." NOT ON PAGE there for specific activities to avoid. metropolitanphysicaltherapy.com/2014/12/23/acute-whiplash-recommendations-and-self-care-instructions gave acute-phase restrictions: "refrain from yoga, weight lifting, and Pilates", "Avoid any heavy lifting and you should generally limit lifting to about 10 pounds", "refrain from vigorous neck stretching. This includes avoiding thrust manipulation"; NOT ON PAGE for injury mechanism. cristchiropractic.com/whiplash-exercises-to-avoid supplied the exercise-level guidance the rules are built on: acute phase "No contact sports", "Avoid running, jumping, or jarring movements", "Limit flexion and extension movements", "Avoid isometric neck exercises"; subacute phase "Avoid overhead presses and heavy squats", "No deadlifts or power cleans", "Avoid football, rugby, and martial arts". Flag: cristchiropractic.com is a chiropractic-clinic blog, not the PubMed/PMC/Physiopedia/AAOS tier the brief asked for first; it was used because the higher-tier sources (Physiopedia, Mayo Clinic, AAOS has no dedicated whiplash page) were unreachable or silent on exercise-level avoidance, and its guidance direction (avoid heavy axial and overhead loading, avoid contact, avoid jarring impact, in a phase-gated way) is consistent with the Cleveland Clinic mechanism and general WAD management literature. No rehab_early exercise was added for whiplash: the acute-phase sources describe what to avoid, not a specific catalog-matched treatment exercise while symptomatic, and existing-rows.json already carries Neck Harness Extension (Four-Way, id 301) as prehab for whiplash, which is a different role.

Stinger/burner (id 61). orthopaedia.com/burners-and-stingers gave the traction/compression mechanism verbatim: "The most common cause of injury is due to traction on the brachial plexus rather than direct trauma. This can occur in ipsilateral shoulder depression and neck deviation towards the contralateral side, often seen in tackling, which causes stretching of the brachial plexus on the ipsilateral side." now.aapmr.org/stingers-and-burners (PM&R KnowledgeNow) corroborated with three mechanisms: "Contralateral lateral neck flexion and/or ipsilateral shoulder depression." (traction), "Neck is forced into ipsilateral lateral flexion and/or oblique extension." (compression), "Blow, often by an opponent's helmet or shoulder, directly over the supraclavicular fossa or lower lateral neck." (direct blow), and treatment guidance: "postural correction, normalization of cervical ROM and flexibility, shoulder strengthening and stabilization", plus "advised against any spearing-type tackling or leading with the head and neck." orthobullets.com/knee-and-sports/3115/burners-and-stingers was reachable but its mechanism detail sat behind a login wall (only "traction injury, compression injury, direct blow" listed with no elaboration). NOT ON PAGE on any of the three sources for a specific exercise-level activity restriction beyond "no spearing tackles" and general return-to-play (symptom-free, full strength/ROM). No rehab_early exercise added: "postural correction... shoulder strengthening and stabilization" is a treatment category, not a named exercise the way McGill's Big Three is for the disc, so no catalog exercise_id could be cited without inventing the connection myself. LEAD NOTE at merge: two whiplash rules dropped (overhead pressing, 31 exercises; heavy squats, deadlifts and cleans, 42). Both rested on a chiropractic clinic page whose only load qualifier is the word heavy, which a name regex cannot express, and they would have removed every barbell squat and deadlift for an acute neck strain. The contact and jumping rules stay with the weak-source flag in their notes.
